title: Chapter 51 – Red Ridge Raid
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

Jian is sitting in the dark under the granary, in a room that does not appear on any plan, when the first footfall comes through the stone.

He feels it before he hears it. It comes up through the soles of his crossed legs, a faint dull tap, like a knuckle on a table in another house. Pebble, in his lap, lifts her head. Her small claws close in the cloth of his sleeve.

Many, she says. Walking. Soft shoes. Not like the cold ones. Like meat.

How many?

I do not count. More than ten. Less than a hundred.

He nods in the dark. It is, for her, a very precise answer.

The room is not large. It is a stone cell, eight paces by five, hollowed out of the hillside two hundred years ago for a purpose nobody recorded. A cold-store, Hu thinks, or a hiding place. It lies under the granary's north wall, reached by a trapdoor in the cellar floor and a ladder of fourteen rungs, and it has no windows and one door, which opens onto a long low tunnel. The tunnel runs north, under the hill, for two hundred and fifty paces, and comes out in the old drainage culvert behind the quarry.

It is the only way into the granary that is not through a wall.

He found it eleven days ago, with the first pulse of Hollow Echo he dared to send in the open, and he has not slept well since.

They are using the culvert, he thinks. Of course they are. He opens his eyes in the dark. It is the one place a man would come, if he did not want to be seen. If he had been told where to look.

Told by whom?

He does not know. He has an idea.

* * *

The Red Ridge steward comes in the dark of the moon, which is a courtesy of sorts.

Zhao Bei is not a subtle man. He is a heavy, deliberate, bull-necked steward of forty-five with a shaved head and a short square beard, and he commands, on behalf of a Patriarch who cannot rise from his bed, a retinue of four hundred. He is a Qi Refining ninth-stage, a peak, and has been for ten years. He is generally considered stuck. He has the manner of a man who has been waiting a very long time for someone to tell him he may stop.

Tonight he has brought thirty. They are not the dull rabble of his usual hired spears. They are his own picked house guards, in dark leather, with short blades, and every third man carries a bundle of sealed pitch and a clay jar of oil. They have crossed the northern pass in three companies, with muffled boots. They have come down the quarry road without a lantern. They are standing now, in the black mouth of the old culvert, with their breaths held, listening to the hill.

Jian knows all of this because Pebble knows it. She has been out, in the last hour, through the one small gap in the cellar wall that Hu left for the drain, and she has returned with her whole body quivering and her nose full of the smell of oil.

Fire, she says. They bring fire. For the big house of bricks. For the place of the old man.

Then they mean to burn the forge.

And everyone who is in it.

His hands are quite steady. He is mildly surprised.

* * *

It is a good plan, as plans go. He has had eleven days to make it.

The culvert is a stone-lined tube, three paces wide and as many high, running straight and level from the quarry's east wall to the granary's north. It is dry. It is smooth. It is perfectly hollow. In all its length there is only one place where a man can stand upright without touching the roof, and that is the long straight section in the middle, one hundred and eighty paces in, where the hill's own rock arches over it in a pale limestone vault.

It is also, as Jian discovered on the third night, completely resonant.

That is the word the interface gave him, when he asked. A closed, regular cavity in dense rock. High Q. It has the kind of voice a hollow thing has when it is struck, a long, pure, singing note that fills the whole tunnel and lasts for twenty breaths. A man standing in it would find his teeth buzzing. He would find his ears ringing. And if somebody, from the far end, were to send a pulse down the length of it, tuned to the note, and pushed, the whole vault would sing itself to pieces.

It is not an attack, he told his father, on the fifth night. It is a tuning. The vault is already cracked. I am only helping it finish.

Wenyuan looked at him for a very long time.

How many will it kill?

I do not know.

How many do you wish it to?

He had not answered. He still has not. It is a question he has been turning over for eleven days, in the dark, with his hands on his knees. He thinks that it is probably the most important one he has ever been asked, and that his father asked it, as he asks everything, gently, without any anger, in the voice of a man who has already taken the answer into himself and is waiting to see whether the boy will do the same.

As few as I can, he said at last.

That is an answer, said Wenyuan. It is not a sum.

It is the best I have.

Then it will do.

* * *

They come down the culvert in a long, silent file.

He feels each one. He cannot see them, but the pulse of the Echo, thrown softly ahead of him, a thread so thin it is barely a whisper, touches them one after another as they pass, and the answer comes back clear. Thirty-one. A shape in each footfall. Qi Refining, mostly fourth or fifth stage, a few sixth, three at the seventh. And at the head of the line, light-footed for his bulk, a thick knot of heat that is Zhao Bei.

He is first, he thinks. Of course he is.

He walks like a man with his hand on a sword, says Pebble, from the dark.

He is. And he is not going to pass the middle.

It is the first lie of the night. The vault will not touch him. He has measured the arc, and the steward will be out of it, three paces from the far end, when the thing begins; the whole weight of it will fall on the thirty behind. It is the only way. If Zhao Bei dies, Red Ridge will come with every man it has, and a steward who lives has somewhere to run, and a story to tell, and a reason to be afraid.

It is not mercy, he tells himself. It is arithmetic.

You keep saying that, says Pebble.

It keeps being true.

Hmm, she says, not convinced.

The first of the file reaches the vault.

He gives it ten breaths. Fifteen. The line of heat grows, spreads, fills the long arch of the limestone with the soft shuffling pressure of thirty bodies in the dark. They are bunching. They are, he sees, in his mind's eye, with great clarity, perfectly arranged, a long double rank, shoulder to shoulder, under the one place in the tunnel where the stone is thin.

Now, he thinks.

* * *

He does not strike the wall. He strikes the note.

It is the thing the stele taught him, in nine days of sitting. You do not hit the empty place; you sing to it. He puts both palms flat on the floor of the hidden cell. He closes his eyes. He gathers, with great care, a thread of Qi as thick as his finger, and pours into it the long deep tone of the vault, and lets it go.

The hill answers.

It begins as a hum. It rises in his own bones, in his teeth, in the soles of his feet. It is a low, steady, patient sound, like a hand drawn across the strings of a great bass instrument, and it fills the whole of the tunnel in a single breath, from end to end. In the vault, thirty men stop walking. He feels their confusion. One of them lifts his head and says something, a small bewildered word.

And then the limestone breaks.

It is not a loud sound. It is a deep one. It goes through him like a thrown spear. The arch of the roof, two hundred years of settled stone, lets go with a sharp long crack, and the first slab comes down on the nearest rank, and the tunnel is full of dust and noise and men.

Then the recoil hits.

He has braced for it. It does not help. It is not a fist this time but a hand, a great flat hand, driving down on his chest from within, pressing every breath out of him, grinding his ribs against his spine. He slides sideways across the stone, with a thin white noise filling his head. For a long time there is only the thudding of his own heart and the hiss of the dust. Pebble is crying out. Her thin high voice is calling his name. He cannot answer.

Breathe, she says. Breathe. Breathe. Breathe.

He breathes.

* * *

When he can see again, a faint amber glow has come into the cell. It is the lamp that Pebble has lit, by some trick of her own, with a pinch of the Orchard's pale dust, and it makes a small warm circle on the stone.

His hands are shaking. Blood is running from his nose, in a thin warm line, over his lip and onto the floor. He wipes it with the back of his wrist. It is not a great deal. It is enough.

```
[ARK-7 — STATUS]
Qi reserve: 3.10 / 11.40.
Hollow Echo (resonance strike): 1 use. Recoil: 1.10.
Acoustic signature: audible to seam-sensitive creatures
within 300 paces. DETECTED: 1 (unclassified, deep).
Warning: Soul strain: mild. Rest recommended.
```

Detected: one. Unclassified. Deep.

He reads the last line twice. He does not like it.

Something heard me, he thinks. Again.

It is not angry, Pebble says, unexpectedly. She is trembling against his side. The cold thing. It is... pleased. A pause. I think it likes the song.

That is not an improvement.

No, she agrees.

He lies there for a time, on the floor of the hidden cell, with the lamp's small circle on the ceiling and the dust still falling in the dark, and does not think about the sound the roof made. Then, with an effort that costs him more than the pulse did, he rolls over onto his hands and knees and begins to crawl toward the door.

* * *

The tunnel is a ruin.

He opens the door a hand's breadth, with Pebble on his shoulder and a needle between his fingers, and the dust rolls out over him in a gray cloud. He coughs. He waits. When the haze thins, he sees it, in the thin gold light of a hooded lantern: the long straight vault, and where it was, a heap.

The middle of the culvert has gone. The roof has fallen in a long cone of broken limestone from wall to wall. At the north end, where the tunnel narrows, a single slab as big as a table has dropped on its own length and lies at a slant, with a hand sticking out from beneath it. The hand is open. It is not moving.

There are bodies. He does not count them. He counts them. Nine. Crushed, or half crushed, in the first thirty paces of the fall. Then, in the rubble, groaning, a long scatter of living, a dozen men in dark leather, half buried, with grit in their hair and blood in their eyes, trying to drag themselves out. Four more have been thrown clear, against the walls, and sit with their backs to the stone and their mouths open, deaf and shocked and silent.

Nine, he thinks. Of thirty-one.

I said as few as I could.

It was not a sum, says the cold part of him, with great gentleness. It was the best I had.

He does not move. A man is crawling toward him over the rubble, a young one, with a torn sleeve and a gash across his scalp, dragging a broken leg. He is perhaps nineteen. He is weeping. He is not looking at Jian. He is looking at the hand, the open one, under the slab, and he says, over and over, in a thin hoarse voice, a name.

Eight left on that side who can still fight, Pebble says. Maybe ten. The big one is gone.

Gone?

Past the middle. At the far end. He ran.

Of course he did. Zhao Bei has not been a steward for ten years by standing in the middle of a collapsing tunnel. Jian has measured him as a man of the sword; he has not measured him as a man of the ear. The vault began to sing, and the steward, who had never in his life heard a stone make a sound like that, did the only thing a man with a Qi sense can do. He ran for the open air.

He will be waiting at the mouth, Jian thinks. With whoever he has left.

He takes a breath. He has three hundred paces to the granary, and nine hundred heartbeats of Qi, and a roll of five needles. He has the Stone Skin talisman his father drew, folded small in his sleeve. He has Pebble.

It will have to do.

* * *

The granary is on fire.

He sees it as he comes up through the cellar trapdoor, in the stifling smoke, with his sleeve over his face: a long red light in the doorway, a roar like a river, black crowds of sparks pouring upward through the roof. Someone has been in. Someone has gone in through the front, while the thirty crawled up the culvert, a second party, smaller, quicker, with pitch and oil.

The diversion, he thinks. It was never the culvert.

He had measured the wrong door.

"Jian!"

It is Hu. The old man is standing at the heart of the great hall, in a ring of fire, with his bent rod in his one hand and his gray beard singed to the chin. The floor around him is a sheet of burning oil. The forge behind him is a roaring mouth. Along the east wall, three young refiners lie in a heap, dazed or dead, and over them, a man in black leather with a short sword and a face like a hatchet is standing with the point at Hu's throat.

"The boy!" Hu cries. "Get out! Get—"

The man with the sword does not look round. He drives the blade forward.

It does not go in.

There is a flat, bright clang, as of a bell being struck, and the old man stumbles back, and a short, heavy, grim figure drops out of the smoke on the swordsman's flank and puts an elbow in his throat. The man folds. A spade of a fist comes down on the back of his head.

"I thought," says Wenshi, in a voice like gravel, "that I had told you to stay in the cellar."

"I did," says Jian.

"You did not stay put."

"No."

"Hm." The Patriarch's brother rubs his bad wrist. His face is gray with soot and smoke. In his left hand, crumpled to a gray rag, is the remnant of a thin yellow slip. The Stone Skin talisman is gone. It has taken a sword-thrust meant for Hu's throat, a hard one, and burned out in the taking. "I will say this. It's a very good talisman."

"My father drew it."

"It's a very good father." Wenshi turns his head. "Where are the rest of them?"

"In the culvert. Some of them."

"Some."

"Nine, I think. Under the roof."

For a moment the big man says nothing. He is looking at the boy, in the red light of the fire, and his dark eyes are very still. Then he says, quite gently: "That is a lot of men."

"Yes."

"Did you want to?"

"No."

"Good." He claps a hand on Jian's shoulder, and it is very heavy, and very warm. "Then that is something. Now go and get the old fool a bucket, before he burns down what's left of the roof."

* * *

They save the forge.

It takes an hour. There are forty of them with buckets, and a long chain from the stream, and the old oak door torn from the cellar and used as a screen. Hu sits against the wall at the end of it, black-faced and wheezing, with his burned hand held up like a child's. Wenshi, with a rib cracked and the old break in his wrist reopened, lets Qinghe bind him and does not make a sound. By the third hour the fire is out. By the fourth, in the gray light before dawn, the last of the Red Ridge raiders, nineteen in all, bound and sullen, are sitting in a row along the guardhouse wall.

The steward is not among them.

Wenyuan questions them himself, at sunrise, in the guardhouse yard, standing, with his hands behind his back.

He does not shout. He has never shouted. He walks slowly down the line, and the nineteen men look up at him with the dull sullen fear of the beaten, and at the end of it he stops in front of the boy with the broken leg. The one who wept. He is, Jian sees from the doorway, even younger than he looked in the dust: a thin brown boy with a country face and one eyebrow cut in two by an old scar.

"What is your name?"

The boy swallows. "Zhao Lin, sir."

"You are Red Ridge?"

"My father is a tenant. I was... They said it was a night's work. Eight stones. They said nobody would be hurt." His voice cracks. "My cousin was behind me. In the tunnel."

"I know." Wenyuan's tone is level. "He is being brought out now. He is alive."

The boy stares. "He is?"

"He has a broken arm. He will have a good scar." The Patriarch looks down the line. "I have not much to say to the rest of you. You came here to burn a granary with four people inside it, on a night with no moon, for a steward who ran. I do not forgive that. I do not pretend to. But I have no wish to hang nineteen men who were paid by the night." He nods to Wenshi, who has been leaning on the gate with a splint on his arm. "You will be fed. Your wounds will be seen to. In three days, you will go home, and you will tell your Patriarch that the Lin clan has taken nothing and killed nothing that was not placed in its road."

A murmur goes down the line.

"Why?" says Zhao Lin, hoarsely. It seems to be the only word he has.

"Because I would like it known," says Wenyuan, "that a man who comes to Green Pine can leave." He turns away. "Though not twice."

* * *

It is later, in the cool of the afternoon, that Qinghe finds him in the shadow of the burned doorway.

She has not slept. She has bandaged thirty-one men, nine of them her own. There is a long smear of soot along her jaw, and the neat knot of her hair has come half undone. She looks, he thinks, like a woman who has spent a night being very strong for a great many people and has at last found a corner in which to stop.

"Sit," she says.

He sits.

She takes his wrist in two cool fingers, and he knows what she is doing, and lets her. The pulse of the blood is steady. The thin fine tremor that has run through his hands since the night of the quarry is almost gone, and in its place is a deep, slow ache, behind the eyes and under the ribs, like a bruise a great way down.

"Soul strain," she says. "Mild. It will pass in two days if you do not touch the Echo."

"Yes."

"You will not touch the Echo."

"No."

"You will say that to my face again, in two days, and mean it."

"Yes, Mother."

She looks at him for a long moment. There is nothing in her face but the plain bone-deep weariness of a woman who has done what she could. And then, with a small jerk, as if something has given way, she lays her forehead against his shoulder, and stays there.

He does not move. He does not think of anything. After a time he puts one hand, awkwardly, on her back.

"You went," she says, into his sleeve. "Into the tunnel. Alone."

"It was the only way."

"I know. I have been doing the sum all night. It was the only way." Her voice is quite steady. "And I want you to know that I have never in my life been so angry."

"I know."

"Not with you."

"I know that too."

She laughs, a short broken sound. Then she lifts her head, and wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand, and is for a moment only a tired woman in a smoky yard, with a small scaled creature sitting at her foot, looking up at her with grave black eyes.

"Pebble says," says Jian, carefully, "that she is very sorry about the fire."

"Does she?"

"She says it was the smell that made her cough."

"Tell her I forgive her." The ghost of a smile touches Qinghe's mouth. "Tell her that she is the only creature on this hill who has not asked me, once, what it costs."

* * *

He sleeps, finally, for six hours, in his own bed, with the shutters open and the sound of hammers drifting up from the burned granary, where forty men are already putting up new rafters. He does not dream. When he wakes it is evening, and Pebble is asleep on his chest, dull-scaled and snoring faintly. Someone has left a bowl of rice porridge on the sill, still warm, with a single pickled plum on top. He eats it slowly, looking at the sky.

It is not until the sun is well up that Jian finds the note.

It is pinned to the dead wood of the granary door, with a short curved knife. It is written on good paper, in a rough square hand, and it says, in four lines, and a signature he knows:

A friend has told me what is under your hill.

Give it to Red Ridge, and the hill will live.

Keep it, and I will come back with the Blood Shadow.

Zhao Bei.

He reads it three times. He folds it. He puts it in his sleeve.

A friend, he thinks. Told by whom?

He looks up at the gray roof of the granary, where the black rafters rise from the ruin like ribs. And he thinks of an old man's soft voice in the east hall, kind and heavy as warm syrup, saying to no one in particular, at a door: I hope I am wrong. I have never hoped it so hard.

He thinks that the fire was not a diversion for the culvert.

It was a diversion for the note.
